drop.title: The Dots in a Circle, and the Wobble No One Can Pin Down

title: The Dots in a Circle,
and the Wobble
No One Can Pin Down
slides.dek: How many ways can a number be a sum of two squares? Its divisors decide. Add those counts across a whole disc and you get πR², plus an error that has stayed open for nearly two centuries.

slides.body: Ask how many ways a number is a sum of two squares, counted honestly, with sign and with order, so 5 = 1² + 2² is *eight* ways, not one. It looks like it should be as unruly as the primes. It is not. Sort the divisors of n by their remainder mod 4: let d₁ count those ≡ 1 and d₃ those ≡ 3. Then *r₂(n) = 4·(d₁ − d₃)*, Jacobi's theorem, 1834. Take 25: divisors 1, 5, 25 are all ≡ 1, so r₂ = 12. Take 21 = 3·7: the two classes cancel, the count is zero, and the circle threads no lattice point. Fermat's yes-or-no rule is just whether that difference is zero.

Jacobi counts the points on *one* circle. Gauss asked the bigger thing: how many lattice points lie *inside* a disc of radius R? Give every point the unit square below and left of it; those squares tile the plane and very nearly cover the disc, so the count is very nearly the *area*, N(R) ≈ πR². And the two views are one: N(R) is exactly 1 plus the sum of r₂(n) over every n up to R². The divisor bookkeeping, summed, *is* the area of a circle. A disc of radius 100 holds 31,417 points against an area of 31,415.9. Close, but it never quite lands. It wobbles.

lines.sub: reopen number theory (idle since #043 two-squares, eleven drops) and rotate format back to research after app #054. the sequel two-squares left open: it asked whether a number is a sum of two squares; this asks how many ways, and the answer is fixed entirely by the number's divisors

three modules over integer-exact engines: a divisor-tally where r₂(n)=4(d₁−d₃) is cross-checked live against every signed, ordered lattice point on the circle of radius √n; a disc-fill racing N(R) against πR²; and the open-problem payoff, the gauss circle error E(R)=N(R)−πR²

checked offline first, 0 mismatches: jacobi's r₂(n) equals a direct signed-and-ordered lattice count for every n from 1 to 20,000; N(R) equals 1 + Σ r₂(n) exactly at R=10/25/50/100. the naive log-log slope of the error is a trap, range-unstable and pre-asymptotic, so console 03 normalises the running-max by three powers of R instead of fitting a line

slides.big:
how many dots
fit in a circle?
*open since 1837.*
slides.sub: Dial n and watch its divisors split into two columns while the circle of radius √n lights every signed, ordered point, r₂(n) = 4(d₁ − d₃), the same fact told twice and always agreeing. Fill a disc and race the count against πR². Then measure the error live and divide it by three powers of R: over √R it climbs, over R it collapses, over R^0.6298 it sits nearly flat. The true exponent is trapped in [½, 0.6298] and no finite plot can name it, which is exactly why a question a child can state has stayed open for nearly two centuries.
